claim: Thirty-one healthy male participants performed a restless four-armed bandit task in a within-subjects design under three drug conditions: 150 mg of the dopamine precursor L-dopa, 2 mg of the D2 receptor antagonist haloperidol, and placebo.
source: Thirty-one healthy male participants performed a restless four-armed bandit task in a within-subjects design under three drug conditions: 150 mg of the dopamine precursor L-dopa, 2 mg of the D2 receptor antagonist haloperidol, and placebo.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design and sample from the abstract.

claim: Choices were best explained by an extension of an established Bayesian learning model accounting for perseveration, directed exploration and random exploration.
source: Choices were best explained by an extension of an established Bayesian learning model accounting for perseveration, directed exploration and random exploration.
evidence: This claim is supported by model comparison results showing the Bayes-SMEP model had highest predictive accuracy.

claim: L-dopa attenuated directed exploration.
source: Modeling revealed attenuated directed exploration under L-dopa, while neural signatures of exploration, exploitation and prediction error were unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by computational modeling results showing reduced directed exploration parameter and percentage of directed exploration trials under L-dopa.

claim: Neural signatures of exploration, exploitation and prediction error were unaffected by L-dopa.
source: Modeling revealed attenuated directed exploration under L-dopa, while neural signatures of exploration, exploitation and prediction error were unaffected.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analyses showing no significant drug effects on exploration/exploitation-related brain activation.

claim: L-dopa attenuated neural representations of overall uncertainty in insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Instead, L-dopa attenuated neural representations of overall uncertainty in insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis showing reduced correlation between overall uncertainty and brain activity in these regions under L-dopa compared to placebo.

claim: Dopamine modulates how insula and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex track accumulating uncertainty during decision-making.
source: Our results highlight the computational role of these regions in exploration and suggest that dopamine modulates how this circuit tracks accumulating uncertainty during decision-making.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observed L-dopa effects on uncertainty-related neural activity.

claim: Striking a balance between exploration and exploitation is essential for maximizing rewards and minimizing costs in the long term.
source: Striking a balance between exploration and exploitation is essential for maximizing rewards and minimizing costs in the long term (Addicott et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Too much exploitation prevents an agent from gathering new information in a volatile environment, and fosters inflexibility and habit formation.
source: Too much exploitation prevents an agent from gathering new information in a volatile environment, and fosters inflexibility and habit formation.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on established understanding of explore/exploit trade-offs.

claim: Too much exploration may lead to inefficient and inconsistent decision-making, thereby reducing long-term payoffs.
source: Too much exploration, on the other hand, may lead to inefficient and inconsistent decision-making, thereby reducing long-term payoffs (Beeler et al., 2014; Addicott et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The restless bandit paradigm uses continuous, slowly drifting rewards for each bandit that encourage participants to strike a balance between exploiting the currently best option and exploring alternative bandits.
source: The restless bandit paradigm uses continuous, slowly drifting rewards for each bandit that encourage participants to strike a balance between exploiting the currently best option and exploring alternative bandits to keep track of their evolving rewards (Daw et al., 2006; Addicott et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the task structure and is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Striatal phasic DA release is tightly linked to reward learning based on reward prediction errors (RPEs).
source: Striatal phasic DA release is tightly linked to reward learning based on reward prediction errors (RPEs) (Steinberg et al., 2013) that reflect differences between experienced and expected outcomes, and serve as a 'teaching signal' that update value predictions (Schultz et al., 1997; Schultz, 2016; Tsai et al., 2009; Glimcher, 2011; Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Reward prediction errors reflect differences between experienced and expected outcomes, and serve as a 'teaching signal' that update value predictions.
source: Striatal phasic DA release is tightly linked to reward learning based on reward prediction errors (RPEs) (Steinberg et al., 2013) that reflect differences between experienced and expected outcomes, and serve as a 'teaching signal' that update value predictions (Schultz et al., 1997; Schultz, 2016; Tsai et al., 2009; Glimcher, 2011; Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a well-established concept in reinforcement learning supported by multiple citations.

claim: Exploitation has been linked to polymorphisms in genes controlling striatal DA signaling, namely the DRD2 gene and the DARPP-32 gene.
source: Exploitation has been linked to polymorphisms in genes controlling striatal DA signaling, namely the DRD2 gene (Frank et al., 2009) predictive of striatal D2 receptor availability (Hirvonen et al., 2004), and the DARPP-32 gene involved in striatal D1 receptor-mediated synaptic plasticity and reward learning (e.g. Calabresi et al., 2000; Stipanovich et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous genetic studies.

claim: Dopamine-transporter (DAT) knockdown mice that are characterized by increased striatal levels of tonic DA showed higher random exploration compared to wild-type controls.
source: Beeler et al., 2010 found that dopamine-transporter (DAT) knockdown mice that are characterized by increased striatal levels of tonic DA (Zhuang et al., 2001) showed higher random exploration compared to wild-type controls.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a specific animal study.

claim: Both directed and random exploration have been associated with variations in the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) gene that modulates prefrontal DAergic tone.
source: In humans, both directed and random exploration have been associated with variations in the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) gene (Kayser et al., 2015; Gershman and Tzovaras, 2018) that modulates prefrontal DAergic tone (Meyer-Lindenberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous genetic studies in humans.

claim: Participants with putatively higher prefrontal DA tone had highest levels of exploration.
source: Participants with putatively higher prefrontal DA tone had highest levels of exploration.
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies on COMT gene variations.

claim: Frontopolar cortex (FPC) is activated during exploratory choices, possibly facilitating behavioral switching between an exploitative and exploratory mode.
source: Daw et al., 2006 showed that frontopolar cortex (FPC) is activated during exploratory choices, possibly facilitating behavioral switching between an exploitative and exploratory mode by overriding value-driven choice tendencies (Daw et al., 2006; Badre et al., 2012; Addicott et al., 2014; Mansouri et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Up- and down-regulation of FPC excitability via transcranial direct current stimulation (TDCS) increases and decreases exploration during reward-based learning.
source: In line with this idea, up- and down-regulation of FPC excitability via transcranial direct current stimulation (TDCS) increases and decreases exploration during reward-based learning (Raja Beharelle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a brain stimulation study.

claim: Anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and anterior insula (AI) have been implicated in exploration.
source: Anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and anterior insula (AI), have also been implicated in exploration (Addicott et al., 2014; Laureiro-Martínez et al., 2014; Laureiro-Martínez et al., 2015; Blanchard and Gershman, 2018), although their precise computational role remains elusive (Blanchard and Gershman, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: ACC and AI may trigger attentional reallocation to salient choice options in the light of increasing uncertainty.
source: Both regions may trigger attentional reallocation to salient choice options in the light of increasing uncertainty (Laureiro-Martínez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the function of these regions supported by citation.

claim: Exploitation is thought to be predominantly supported by structures within a 'valuation' network including ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), ventral striatum and hippocampus.
source: Exploitation, on the other hand, is thought to be predominantly supported by structures within a 'valuation' network including ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), ventral striatum and hippocampus (Daw et al., 2006; Bartra et al., 2013; Clithero and Rangel, 2014; Laureiro-Martínez et al., 2014; Laureiro-Martínez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: L-dopa is thought to stimulate DA transmission by providing increased substrate for DA synthesis.
source: While L-dopa is thought to stimulate DA transmission by providing increased substrate for DA synthesis, haloperidol reduces DA transmission by blocking D2 receptors.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of action of L-dopa based on established pharmacology.

claim: Haloperidol reduces DA transmission by blocking D2 receptors.
source: While L-dopa is thought to stimulate DA transmission by providing increased substrate for DA synthesis, haloperidol reduces DA transmission by blocking D2 receptors.
evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of action of haloperidol based on established pharmacology.

claim: Haloperidol might also increase DA release via action on presynaptic D2 autoreceptors.
source: However, we note that Haloperidol might also increase DA release via action on presynaptic D2 autoreceptors (z.B. Frank and O'Reilly, 2006).
evidence: This is a caveat about haloperidol's mechanism supported by citation.

claim: Participants' choice behavior indicated that they understood the task structure, and tracked the most valuable bandit throughout the task.
source: Overall, participants' choice behavior indicated that they understood the task structure, and tracked the most valuable bandit throughout the task (see Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data showing above-chance selection of the best bandit.

claim: On trial 1, participants randomly selected one of the four bandits with a probability of 21.5 ± 7.49%.
source: On trial 1, participants randomly selected one of the four bandits (probability to choose best bandit: 21.5 ± 7.49%, M ± SE).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the behavioral data.

claim: After five trials, participants selected the most valuable option with 49.03% (±4.98%), which was significantly above chance level of 25%.
source: After five trials, participants already selected the most valuable option with 49.03% (±4.98%; M ± SE), which was significantly above chance level of 25% (t30 = 4.83, p=3.82*10−5, Figure 2), and consistently kept choosing the bandit with the highest payoff with on average 67.89% (±2.78%).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Participants consistently kept choosing the bandit with the highest payoff with on average 67.89% (±2.78%).
source: After five trials, participants already selected the most valuable option with 49.03% (±4.98%; M ± SE), which was significantly above chance level of 25% (t30 = 4.83, p=3.82*10−5, Figure 2), and consistently kept choosing the bandit with the highest payoff with on average 67.89% (±2.78%).
evidence: This is a descriptive statistic from the behavioral data.

claim: There were no significant drug effects on overall monetary payout, percentage of choices of the best bandit, percentage of choice switches, or median reaction times.
source: Yet, rmANOVAs yielded no significant drug effect on any of these four model-free choice variables (payout: F2,60=0.06, p=0.943; %bestbandit: F2,60=0.34, p=0.711; %switches: F2,60=1.02, p=0.366; median RT: F2,60=0.50, p=0.611).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis showing no significant effects.

claim: The Bayesian learning model with terms for directed exploration and perseveration (Bayes-SMEP) showed highest predictive accuracy in each drug condition and overall.
source: The Bayesian learning model with terms for directed exploration and perseveration (Bayes-SMEP) showed highest predictive accuracy in each drug condition and overall (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by leave-one-out cross-validation model comparison results.

claim: There was a significant drug effect on the percentage of directed explorations.
source: We found a significant drug effect only for the percentage of directed explorations (F1.66,49.91=7.18, p=.003; Figure 5c).
evidence: This is supported by repeated measures ANOVA results.

claim: The percentage of random explorations was not significantly modulated by drug.
source: The percentage of random explorations (F2,60=0.55, p=.58, Figure 5b) or exploitations (F2,60=1.57, p=.22; Figure 5a) were not significantly modulated by drug.
evidence: This is supported by repeated measures ANOVA results.

claim: The percentage of exploitations was not significantly modulated by drug.
source: The percentage of random explorations (F2,60=0.55, p=.58, Figure 5b) or exploitations (F2,60=1.57, p=.22; Figure 5a) were not significantly modulated by drug.
evidence: This is supported by repeated measures ANOVA results.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the percentage of directed explorations under L-dopa compared to placebo.
source: Post-hoc, paired t-tests showed a significant reduction in the percentage of directed explorations under L-dopa compared to placebo (mean difference P-D=2.82, t30=4.69, p<.001) and haloperidol (mean difference H-D = 2.42, t30=2.76, p=.010), but not between placebo and haloperidol (mean difference P-H=0.39, t30=0.43, p=.667).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc paired t-tests.

claim: There was a significant reduction in the percentage of directed explorations under L-dopa compared to haloperidol.
source: Post-hoc, paired t-tests showed a significant reduction in the percentage of directed explorations under L-dopa compared to placebo (mean difference P-D=2.82, t30=4.69, p<.001) and haloperidol (mean difference H-D = 2.42, t30=2.76, p=.010), but not between placebo and haloperidol (mean difference P-H=0.39, t30=0.43, p=.667).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc paired t-tests.

claim: There was no significant difference in the percentage of directed explorations between placebo and haloperidol.
source: Post-hoc, paired t-tests showed a significant reduction in the percentage of directed explorations under L-dopa compared to placebo (mean difference P-D=2.82, t30=4.69, p<.001) and haloperidol (mean difference H-D = 2.42, t30=2.76, p=.010), but not between placebo and haloperidol (mean difference P-H=0.39, t30=0.43, p=.667).
evidence: This is supported by post-hoc paired t-tests.

claim: The percentage of exploitations was marginally increased under L-dopa compared to placebo.
source: Notably, an exploratory t-test revealed that the percentage of exploitations was marginally increased under L-dopa compared to placebo (mean difference P-D=-2.61, t30=-1.92, p=.065).
evidence: This is supported by an exploratory t-test showing a trend-level effect.

claim: No effects of L-dopa were observed on random exploration (β) or perseveration (ρ).
source: In contrast, we did not observe effects of L-dopa on random exploration (β, Figure 6) or perseveration (ρ, Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical Bayesian modeling results.

claim: Haloperidol showed no effects on the posterior group-level means of any parameter.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, haloperidol showed no effects on the posterior group-level means of any parameter.
evidence: This is supported by hierarchical Bayesian modeling results.

claim: Exploratory choices were associated with higher activity in bilateral frontopolar cortex (FPC), bilateral intraparietal sulcus (IPS), bilateral anterior insula (AI), and dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC).
source: Replicating earlier findings (e.g. Daw et al., 2006; Addicott et al., 2014), exploration trials were associated with greater activation in bilateral frontopolar cortex (FPC; left: −42, 27, 27 mm; z = 6.07; right: 39, 34, 28 mm; z = 7.56), in a large cluster along the bilateral intraparietal sulcus (IPS; cluster peak at −48,–33, 52; z = 10.45), and in bilateral anterior insula (AI; left: −36, 15, 3 mm; z = 6.69; right: 36, 20, 3 mm; z = 6.87) as well as dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC; cluster peak at 8, 12, 45 mm; z = 8.47).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis comparing exploration vs. exploitation trials.

claim: Exploitative choices were associated with greater activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) and bilateral lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC).
source: In contrast, exploitative choices were associated with greater activation in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC; −2, 40,–10 mm; z = 5.67) and in bilateral lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC; left: −38, 34,–14 mm; z = 5.81; right: 38, 36,–12 mm; z = 5.02).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis comparing exploitation vs. exploration trials.

claim: Greater activation during exploitative trials was observed in a cluster spanning the left posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and left precuneus.
source: Furthermore, greater activation during exploitative trials was also observed in a cluster spanning the left posterior cingulate cortex (PCC) and left precuneus (cluster peak at −6,–52, 15 mm; z = 7.40), as well as in the angular gyrus (left: −42,–74, 34 mm; z = 8.04; right: 52,–68, 28 mm; z = 7.02), hippocampus (left: −24,–16, −15 mm; z = 4.16; only at p<0.001, uncorrected; right: 32,–16, −15 mm; z = 5.09), and several clusters along the superior and middle temporal gyrus.
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis comparing exploitation vs. exploration trials.

claim: No differential activation patterns were observed for directed and random exploration types.
source: We observed no differential activation patterns for directed and random exploration types when expanding the original trial classification of Daw et al., 2006 in a third GLM (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis comparing directed vs. random exploration.

claim: No main effect of drug on differential explore/exploit-related brain activation was found.
source: Surprisingly, we found no suprathreshold activations on the whole-brain level, nor in any of seven regions of interest (ROIs) with small volume correction applied (i.e. left/right FPC, left/right IPS, left/right AI, and dACC).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis testing for drug effects on exploration/exploitation-related activation.

claim: No drug effects were found on neural activation at trial onset, reward onset, PE, and outcome value.
source: Likewise, further analyses revealed no drug effects on neural activation (trial onset, reward onset, PE, and outcome value; see Appendix 1 for details) and no evidence for an association of drug effects with putative proxy measures of baseline DA availability (spontaneous blink rate and working memory span, see Appendix 1 for details).
evidence: This is supported by additional fMRI analyses reported in the appendix.

claim: In the placebo condition, activity in the bilateral dACC, right anterior insula, and left posterior insula was positively correlated with overall uncertainty.
source: In the placebo condition alone, no voxels survived whole-brain FWE correction (p<.05), but a more lenient threshold (p<.001, uncorrected) revealed activity in the bilateral dACC (cluster peak at -3, 21, 39mm; z=3.96), right anterior insula (42, 15, -6mm; z=3.46), and left posterior insula (PI) (-34, -20, 8mm; z=4.63) that was positively correlated with the overall uncertainty (Figure 8a, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis using overall uncertainty as a parametric regressor.

claim: L-dopa reduced uncertainty-related activity in the left posterior insula compared to placebo.
source: While the contrast L-dopa>placebo yielded no suprathreshold activations, the reverse contrast (placebo>L-dopa) revealed a significant activation in the left PI (-34, -20, 8mm; z=5.05).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis comparing drug effects on overall uncertainty-related activation.

claim: At a reduced threshold, left AI and bilateral dACC showed a stronger correlation with overall uncertainty under placebo compared to L-dopa.
source: At a reduced threshold (p<.001, uncorrected), left AI (-38, 6, 14mm; z=4.88) and bilateral dACC (left: -2, 36, 33mm; z=3.32; right: 4, 14, 28mm; z=3.41) showed a stronger correlation with the overall uncertainty under placebo compared to L-dopa (Figure 8b, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by fMRI analysis comparing drug effects on overall uncertainty-related activation.

claim: L-dopa primarily increases phasic rather than tonic striatal DA activity.
source: PET studies in humans also indicate that L-dopa primarily increases phasic rather than tonic striatal DA activity (Floel et al., 2008; Black et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to PET imaging studies.

claim: Increased phasic DA release was associated with improved learning under L-dopa compared to placebo, presumably by enhancing the reinforcing effect of positive feedback during learning.
source: Increased phasic DA release was associated with improved learning under L-dopa compared to placebo, presumably by enhancing the reinforcing effect of positive feedback during learning (Frank et al., 2004; Pessiglione et al., 2006; Cox et al., 2015; Mathar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous pharmacological studies.

claim: L-dopa might strengthen positive reinforcing effects of immediate rewards via increased phasic striatal DA release, fostering both impulsive and exploitative choice behavior.
source: Thus, L-dopa might strengthen-positive reinforcing effects of immediate rewards (Pine et al., 2010) via increased phasic striatal DA release, fostering both impulsive and exploitative choice behavior (Kobayashi and Schultz, 2008; Schultz, 2010; Pine et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on previous literature and the current findings.

claim: L-dopa might have attenuated exploration via indirectly modulating frontal activity through bottom-up interference.
source: Thus, L-dopa might have also attenuated exploration via indirectly modulating frontal activity through bottom-up interference (Kellendonk et al., 2006; Simpson et al., 2010; Kohno et al., 2015; Duvarci et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Low doses of D2 antagonists can stimulate DA signaling, possibly via acting on presynaptic auto-receptors.
source: Low doses of D2 antagonists can stimulate DA signaling, possibly via acting on presynaptic auto-receptors (Schmitz et al., 2003; Frank and O'Reilly, 2006; Ford, 2014), which contrasts with the antidopaminergic effects observed under chronic and high-dose treatment (Starke et al., 1989; Frank and O'Reilly, 2006; Knutson and Gibbs, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to pharmacological studies.

claim: Insula and dACC are thought to form a salience network involved in detecting and orienting toward salient stimuli.
source: The dACC and AI, on the other hand, are thought to form a salience network involved in detecting and orienting toward salient stimuli (Menon, 2015; Uddin, 2015), which may also subserve attentional and behavioral switching from exploitation to exploration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on brain networks.

claim: vmPFC and OFC are implicated in coding the subjective value of attainable goods.
source: Both regions are implicated in coding the subjective value of attainable goods (Levy and Glimcher, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The insula plays a key role for integrating interoceptive signals about bodily states into conscious feelings that can influence decision-making under risk and uncertainty.
source: The insula is also considered to play a key role for integrating interoceptive signals about bodily states into conscious feelings, such as urgency, that can influence decision-making under risk and uncertainty (Craig, 2002; Craig, 2009; Critchley, 2005; Naqvi and Bechara, 2009; Singer et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on insula function.

claim: The ACC monitors response conflict and triggers attentional and behavioral changes for reducing future conflict.
source: The ACC is known to monitor response conflict, which should increase with the overall uncertainty, and to trigger attentional and behavioral changes for reducing future conflict (Botvinick et al., 2004; Kerns et al., 2004; Vanveen and Carter, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on ACC function.

claim: Expression of D1 and D2 receptors is much higher in striatum than in insula and ACC.
source: Expression of D1 and D2 receptors is much higher in striatum than in insula and ACC (Hall et al., 1994; Hurd et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroanatomical studies.

claim: L-dopa may have affected uncertainty-related activity in the insula and ACC indirectly by modulating DA transmission on the striatal level.
source: Hence, L-dopa may have affected uncertainty-related activity in the insula and ACC indirectly by modulating DA transmission on the striatal level.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on receptor distribution and the observed effects.

claim: L-dopa might have modulated striatal processing of reward uncertainty that is subsequently transmitted to cortical structures for integration with other decision parameters to guide explore/exploit behavior.
source: More specifically, L-dopa might have modulated striatal processing of reward uncertainty (Preuschoff et al., 2006; Schultz et al., 2008) that subsequently is transmitted to cortical structures for integration with other decision parameters to guide explore/exploit behavior (Kennerley et al., 2006; Rushworth and Behrens, 2008; Haber and Knutson, 2010; Shenhav et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The moderate sample size of 31 subjects may have contributed to the absence of haloperidol effects and the absence of drug-associated differences in categorical contrasts of explore/exploit trials in the fMRI analysis.
source: In addition to the limitations discussed above, the moderate sample size of 31 subjects in this within-subjects manipulation study may have contributed to the absence of haloperidol effects and the absence of drug-associated differences in categorical contrasts of explore/exploit trials in the fMRI analysis.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation related to statistical power.

claim: The BOLD signal provides an indirect index of blood oxygenation rather than a direct measure of DA activity.
source: Needless to say, the BOLD signal provides an indirect index of blood oxygenation rather than a direct measure of DA activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of the fMRI measurement based on established knowledge.

claim: An observed BOLD signal change must not necessarily rely on a change in DA transmission, and a change in DA transmission must not necessarily produce a (detectable) BOLD signal change.
source: Hence, an observed BOLD signal change must not necessarily rely on a change in DA transmission, and a change in DA transmission must not necessarily produce a (detectable) BOLD signal change (Brocka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a caveat about interpreting BOLD signals supported by citation.

claim: Humans use both random and directed exploration to solve the explore/exploit tradeoff.
source: First, our cognitive modeling results confirm that humans use both random and directed exploration to solve the explore/exploit tradeoff.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model comparison results.

claim: Accounting for choice perseveration improves model fit and interpretability of the parameter capturing directed exploration.
source: Notably, we extend previous findings by showing that accounting for choice perseveration improves model fit and interpretability of the parameter capturing directed exploration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the model comparison results.

claim: DA is causally involved in the explore/exploit trade-off in humans by regulating the extent to which subjects engage in directed exploration.
source: Our results support the notion that DA is causally involved in the explore/exploit trade-off in humans by regulating the extent to which subjects engage in directed exploration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the L-dopa effects on directed exploration.

claim: DA does not control the explore/exploit trade-off by modulating the neural signatures of exploratory and exploitative decisions per se.
source: Interestingly, our neuroimaging data do not support the hypothesis that DA controls this trade-off by modulating the neural signatures of exploratory and exploitative decisions per se.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the absence of drug effects on exploration/exploitation-related brain activation.

claim: DA modulates tracking of overall uncertainty in a cortical control network comprising the insula and dACC, which might then drive exploration in the face of accumulating uncertainty.
source: In contrast, we provide first evidence that DA modulates tracking of overall uncertainty in a cortical control network comprising the insula and dACC, which might then drive exploration in the face of accumulating uncertainty.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the L-dopa effects on uncertainty-related brain activation.

claim: Only males were included in the study because female sex hormones fluctuate during menstrual cycle which may affect DA signaling.
source: Only males were included, as female sex hormones fluctuate during menstrual cycle which may affect DA signaling (Almey et al., 2015; Yoest et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a methodological decision supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sample-size (n = 31, within-subject design) was based on previous work regarding exploration-related brain activation and dopaminergic manipulation of reinforcement learning.
source: Sample-size (n = 31, within-subject design) was based on previous work regarding exploration-related brain activation (Daw et al., 2006; n = 14), and dopaminergic manipulation of reinforcement learning (Pessiglione et al., 2006; n = 13, between-subject design).
evidence: This is a methodological justification based on previous studies.

claim: The study procedures were approved by the local ethics committee (Hamburg Medical Council).
source: The study procedures were approved by the local ethics committee (Hamburg Medical Council).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Each subject was tested in four separate sessions: one baseline session and three fMRI sessions.
source: Each subject (n = 31) was tested in four separate sessions: one baseline session and three fMRI sessions.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The mean payoffs of the four bandits drifted randomly across trials according to a decaying Gaussian random walk.
source: The mean payoffs of the four bandits drifted randomly across trials according to a decaying Gaussian random walk.
evidence: This is a description of the task structure.

claim: The Kalman filter assumes that subjects form an internal representation of the true underlying reward structure of the task.
source: The model assumes that subjects form an internal representation of the true underlying reward structure of the task.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model's assumptions.

claim: According to the model, participants update their reward expectations of the chosen bandit according to Bayes' theorem.
source: According to the model, participants update their reward expectations of the chosen bandit according to Bayes' theorem.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model's learning rule.

claim: The Kalman gain determines the fraction of the prediction error that is used for updating.
source: The Kalman gain determines the fraction of the prediction error that is used for updating.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model's learning mechanism.

claim: Posterior parameter distributions were estimated for each subject and drug condition using hierarchical Bayesian modeling within Stan.
source: Posterior parameter distributions were estimated for each subject and drug condition using hierarchical Bayesian modeling within Stan (version 2.17.0; Stan Development Team, 2017), operating under the general statistical package R (version 3.4.3; R Development Core Team, 2017).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical analysis method.

claim: Preprocessing and statistical analysis of fMRI data was performed using SPM12.
source: Preprocessing and statistical analysis of fMRI data was performed using SPM12 (Wellcome Department of Imaging Neuroscience, London, UK).
evidence: This is a description of the fMRI analysis software.

claim: All fMRI results are reported at a threshold of p<0.05, FWE-corrected for the whole brain volume, unless stated otherwise.
source: All fMRI results are reported at a threshold of p<0.05, FWE-corrected for the whole brain volume, unless stated otherwise.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical threshold used for fMRI results.
